text: Real work rarely involves just one value - it involves lists of them, like a whole set of incident numbers. Arrays are JavaScript's ordered list type, and this lesson covers creating them, measuring them, and the handful of methods you'll reach for constantly.

An array of incident numbers is written in square brackets. Indexing always starts at zero, so the first item sits at index zero, not index one - a common source of off-by-one mistakes for anyone new to the language. The length property tells you how many items are in the array, and the last item always sits at length minus one.

Push adds an item to the end of the array. Pop removes and returns that last item. indexOf searches for a value and gives you back its position - and importantly, if the value isn't found anywhere in the array, indexOf doesn't throw an error, it returns negative one, which is the standard way to check whether something is missing before you decide what to do next.

Three methods come up again and again once you're processing lists of data. forEach simply runs a function once for every item and gives nothing back. map builds and returns a brand-new array where every item has been transformed by your function. And filter also returns a brand-new array, but one that only keeps the items where your function returned true.

Here's filter in action on an array of incident objects: the function checks whether each incident's priority equals one, and criticalOnly ends up holding just the matching incidents. Notice the original incidents array is never touched - map and filter always hand you back a new array rather than modifying the one you started with, which matters once you're processing real result sets from ServiceNow's APIs later in this course.

Indexing from zero, push and pop for the ends of a list, indexOf for searching, and forEach, map, and filter for working across the whole thing. Next up: objects - the shape that ServiceNow records and JSON data both share.
